newsitem.title: UK: UK companies look at pushing up prices - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK companies look at pushing up prices - survey.

text.p: British companies are feeling the benefits of economic recovery and looking at pushing up prices for the first time since emerging from recession, a survey said on Monday.

The survey by the Chartered Institute of Marketing (CMI) said manufacturers and service firms that focussed in the last couple of years on expanding sales were now keen to squeeze higher profits out of existing sales.
"In the early part of the recovery, companies wanted to stay alive. Now they're ready to start pushing prices up," Douglas McWilliams, CMI's economic adviser, said.
"People had been chasing the business and had been prepared to take a hit on the margins in order to get the market share," he told Reuters.
"Now there is enough demand out there and enough sales that people feel they can put their prices up," he said.
McWilliams said the survey showed inflation might be rising soon.
The "Marketing Trends Survey" is a quarterly survey of marketing directors at nearly 200 manufacturing companies and service firms.

The report said companies surveyed expected sales to grow an average 7.3 percent in cash terms in the current financial year, or 5.4 percent in real terms, compared to 7.0 percent in cash terms last year.
Marketing directors surveyed said information systems continued to be the fastest growing part of their budgets, forecast to rise 5.9 in the current financial year.
This was followed by budgets for direct mail, which were expected to grow an average 4.9 percent.

McWilliams said direct mail was growing faster than budgets for advertising, public relations, sponsorship, promotions and telemarketing because companies were increasingly using databases to target customers.
"Advertising, public relations and sponsorship are ways of mass broadcasting your message," he said.
"The overall trend we've seen is a move towards a more focussed way of reaching the customer directly," he said.

McWilliams, whose Centre for Economics and Business Research carried out the survey for the CMI, said marketing directors of companies were more aware of what consumers were buying and why than the finance directors who normally answered similar corporate surveys.
The survey said 54 percent of respondents were happy with the size of their marketing and sales teams, 40 percent planned to increase staff and only seven percent planned to cut back.
